newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hoechst to merge specialty chemicals units.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hoechst to merge specialty chemicals units.

text.p: Hoechst AG, Europe's largest chemicals group, on Tuesday said it plans to merge its flagging specialty chemicals business with Swiss group Clariant AG into a new industry leader but at a cost of heavy job losses.

Hoechst told German bourse authorities it would introduce virtually all of its specialty chemicals business, including pigments and additives as well as other businesses, into a new group and take a minority stake of 40-45 percent in Clariant.

The new group, also called Clariant and expected to be the global industry leader, will post sales of nine billion marks ($5.8 billion) in annual sales, Hoechst board member Karl-Gerhard Seifert told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Acknowledging that Hoechst's specialty chemicals have been an underperformer plagued by restructurings for some time, Seifert said he hopes the new group will be a "very profitable European chemicals group." "The intended plan is for the company to grow in the area of specialty chemicals," he said.
For Hoechst the merger will improve the group's presence in Asia and the U.S. and improve the portfolio Seifert said.
While each company stands to reap enormous savings estimated at around 600 million marks, some 16 percent of all jobs will be lost.
"We expect to cut around 5,000 jobs worldwide over the next three years in a socially acceptable manner," reducing the workforce from 31,000 at the moment, Seifert said.
Although no major plant closures are planned at the moment, Seiftert said he could not rule out such steps in the future as the group does not need to keep its 120 sites operating.
For Hoechst, having made no secret of its hopes to spin-off the specialty chemicals business, the deal further underscores its efforts to focus more on life-sciences, Seifert added.

Hoechst, providing 6.5 billion marks in sales to the new group, said Clariant will remain a Swiss share company, quoted on the Zurich stock exchange. Clariant will bring in 2.7 billion marks in sales into the new group. Seifert could not say whether the new group will pay a dividend next year.
A large portion of the new group's business would be run by a German subsidiary, Hoechst said.

The markets cheered Hoechst's decision, sending shares up 3.56 percent to 71.22 marks in after-hours electronic trading while Clariant shares shot up over 13 percent to 508 Swiss francs after both were briefly suspended from trading.
Clariant, which was spun off from Swiss drugs giant Sandoz AG in 1995, also said that the merger would catapult it into the top position in nearly every business area.
Analysts welcomed the deal, saying Hoechst had taken a bold step in revamping a sector that some analysts believed had been mismanaged for some time.
"This is certainly good news for each of the companies," said Tony Cox, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
He added the move might further improve shareholder value for Hoechst as the group would effectively receive a share market quotation for certain businesses.
Seifert shrugged off the fact that Switzerland, like Germany, is generally plagued by very high costs, saying that Clariant is an internationally diverse group, which helps bring down costs.

Hoechst, one of Germany's most vocal supporters of the concept of shareholder value, in November announced plans to make itself into a strategic management holding company turning its businesses into separate legal entities and seeking bourse listings for some of these groups.
